analysis.one_liner: Fault-based toxic-waste liability, strict numerical cleanup standards and deadlines, and broader corporate taxes to fund cleanups.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in July 1992 with no cosponsors, referred to three House committees and two subcommittees, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have overhauled the Superfund program, which cleans up the nation's worst toxic waste sites. It would have replaced the current blanket liability rule with a fault-based standard — companies could be sued for cleanup costs if they knew or should have known their dumping would endanger health or the environment. It would have required the EPA to set hard numerical cleanup limits for each hazardous chemical, set enforceable deadlines for finishing cleanups with fines for missing them, barred simply capping a waste site in place unless full cleanup is technically impossible, and raised cleanup money by lowering the Superfund corporate tax exemption from $2 million to $1 million of income.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near Superfund sites, who would get faster cleanups under enforceable deadlines, firmer numerical limits on how much toxic residue can remain in soil and water, and a bar on cheap 'cap it and walk away' remedies unless full cleanup is technically impossible. Taxpayers would also benefit from expanded corporate tax revenue dedicated to cleanups.

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA to set numerical cleanup standards — measured in parts per million — for every hazardous substance at Superfund sites, replacing site-by-site judgment calls, and applies those standards to every site on the National Priorities List unless EPA finds them not sufficiently protective or grants a waiver [S2][S3].

Directs EPA to set deadlines for completing site investigation, cleanup design, and actual cleanup, with civil penalties of up to $5,000 per day for missing them — addressing the program's notorious slowness [S2][S3].
Bars the government from choosing to cap a site instead of cleaning it up unless compliance with the numerical standards is not technologically feasible [S2][S3].

Revises Superfund liability to a fault-based standard: owners, operators, and related parent or subsidiary corporations are liable if they knew or should have known their disposal would substantially endanger health or the environment, or if they violated environmental rules in effect at the time [S2][S3].
Broadens the corporate environmental minimum tax by lowering the exemption from $2 million to $1 million of alternative minimum taxable income, raising dedicated cleanup revenue [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that would pay the expanded Superfund minimum tax — including mid-sized companies with over $1 million in alternative minimum taxable income, not just the largest firms. Companies that disposed of hazardous waste would face liability if a case could be shown they knew or should have known of the danger, plus new deadline penalties. Some cleanup compliance costs would likely be passed to consumers.

drawbacks.text: Replacing blanket liability with a fault-based standard makes it harder to collect cleanup costs from companies, since plaintiffs must prove the company knew or should have known of the danger; where fault cannot be shown, more cleanup costs could fall on the public Superfund trust rather than on polluters [S2][S3].

The tax change subjects corporations with alternative minimum taxable income as low as $1 million to the environmental tax, a cost that would fall partly on mid-sized companies and could be passed to consumers [S3].

Rigid numerical standards for every hazardous substance, with waivers only at EPA's discretion, could force enormously expensive cleanups to reach very low contamination levels where the health benefit per dollar is small — the long-standing 'how clean is clean' criticism of Superfund [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For communities near toxic sites, the bill offered real gains: enforceable deadlines, firm cleanup numbers, and a bar on capping sites in place. But the design cuts both ways. The fault-based liability limit — which much of the business community sought in the 1992 Superfund reauthorization fight — makes recovering cleanup costs from polluters harder and could shift costs onto the public trust, partially offsetting the new tax revenue. The combination of strict standards, deadlines, penalties, and a broader tax would have imposed substantial, largely one-size-fits-all costs on industry. It was an attempt to balance polluter liability relief against tougher cleanup requirements, and its death left the slower, vaguer status quo in place.

outcome.mechanism: Referred on introduction to three House committees and then to two subcommittees, none of which acted on it, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Wayne Owens of Utah introduced the bill on July 9, 1992, with no cosponsors [S1][S4].
It was referred the same day to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Public Works and Transportation, and Ways and Means [S5].
Within two weeks it was sent to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials and the Subcommittee on Water Resources; no hearings, markup, or floor vote followed [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and all legislation not passed expired [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that would have paid the broadened Superfund tax and faced hard numerical cleanup standards and daily deadline penalties are better off that the bill died. Communities near Superfund sites lost the chance at faster, more strictly defined cleanups, and the status quo — blanket strict liability alongside slow, discretionary cleanups — remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations that would have paid the broader tax

for.name: Rep. Wayne Owens
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pursued no visible cosponsors before it stalled in committee.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup or scheduled it for floor action.

against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over hazardous waste transport and cleanup
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never acted on it beyond subcommittee referral.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means (chair Rep. Dan Rostenkowski)
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over the tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never acted on its Superfund tax provisions.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred; the bill had one Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and no recorded opposition, so its partisan shape cannot be measured [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Chemical and manufacturing companies with hazardous waste liability
industries.note: The bill's fault-based standard would have limited their exposure compared with blanket strict liability, but they would have faced hard numerical cleanup standards, enforceable deadlines with fines, and a ban on cheap capping remedies. Their liability relief ran against full public cost recovery, while their compliance costs accompanied cleaner sites for nearby residents.

industries.industry: Corporations subject to the Superfund environmental tax
industries.note: The bill would halve the tax exemption from $2 million to $1 million of alternative minimum taxable income, pulling many mid-sized corporations into the tax. That money would have funded cleanups the public benefits from, so the industry's interest ran against the public's in this provision.

Firm numerical standards, deadlines, and a bar on capping sites would have required more and faster full cleanups, expanding demand for remediation work. Their business depends on the cleanups communities want.
